hints: Think about why gallium shows two peaks at 69 and 71, what does an average atom have to take into account?
Recall what standard all relative masses are compared to, and what fraction of that standard is defined as one unit.
walkthrough:
See why an average is needed**
Gallium is not made of identical atoms. Your spectrum shows $^{69}\text{Ga}$ and $^{71}\text{Ga}$ in a roughly 60:40 ratio. So one single atom does not represent the element. You need a weighted average that accounts for the mass and abundance of each isotope.

Fix the comparison standard**
Relative means compared to a standard, with no units. In chemistry that standard is always a carbon-12 atom. One atomic mass unit is defined as exactly 1/12 of the mass of one atom of $^{12}\text{C}$. So you are saying how many times heavier the average gallium atom is than this unit.

Final answer: The (weighted) average mass of an atom of an element
relative to 1/12 of the mass of an atom of $^{12}\text{C}$.

hints: Read the mass and % abundance for each peak from the spectrum and multiply each mass by its fractional or percentage abundance.
Remember to divide the total by 100 if you use percentages, and round the final answer to 4 significant figures.
walkthrough:
Set up the weighted average**
Each isotope contributes mass $\times$ abundance. Add the contributions and divide by total abundance:
$$A_r = \frac{(60.11 \times 69) + (39.89 \times 71)}{100}$$

Calculate and round correctly**
$60.11 \times 69 = 4147.59$ and $39.89 \times 71 = 2832.19$. Sum $= 6979.78$. Divide by 100 gives $69.7978$. To 4 significant figures this is $69.80$. Keep the zero at the end, it shows the precision required.

Final answer: Working: $A_r = \frac{(60.11 \times 69) + (39.89 \times 71)}{100} = 69.7978$
relative atomic mass = $69.80$

hints: Look at the symbol $^{71}\text{Ga}$, what does the top left number tell you about protons plus neutrons?
Write the full electronic configuration of Ga (Z = 31) and count how many electrons sit in n = 1, the lowest energy level.
Identify the last subshell filled for a Group 13 element in Period 4, is the outer electron in an s, p or d orbital?
walkthrough:
Read the nucleon number**
In $^{71}\text{Ga}$, the 71 is the mass number, the total of protons + neutrons in the nucleus. So nucleon number $= 71$. This is independent of electrons.

Count the lowest level electrons**
Gallium has atomic number 31, so a neutral atom has 31 electrons. Configuration is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^{10} 4s^2 4p^1$. The lowest energy level is n = 1, which holds only the $1s^2$ electrons. So total $= 2$.

Find the highest energy electron**
The highest principal quantum number occupied is n = 4. The last electron goes into $4p^1$ because Ga is in Group 13, first element of the p-block in Period 4. So the orbital type containing the highest energy electron is p.
Final answer: nucleon number: $71$; total number of electrons in lowest energy level: $2$; type of orbital in highest energy level: p (-orbital).

hints: Count bonding pairs and lone pairs on Ga in $\text{GaCl}_{3}$, remember Ga is in Group 13 so has 3 outer electrons to share.
Recall the shape and angle that places three bonding pairs as far apart as possible with no lone pair on the central atom.
walkthrough:
Count electron pairs on gallium**
In $\text{GaCl}_{3}$, Ga forms three single $\text{Ga-Cl}$ bonds and has no lone pair left, because its three valence electrons are all used in bonding. So you have 3 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs.

Apply repulsion to get shape and angle**
Three electron pairs repel equally to be as far apart as possible. That gives a flat, trigonal planar arrangement with the three Cl atoms at the corners of a triangle around Ga. The angle between any two bonds is $360^{\circ}/3 = 120^{\circ}$.

Final answer: Shape: trigonal planar with Ga at centre and three Cl arranged symmetrically around it in one plane.
Bond angle $\text{Cl-Ga-Cl} = 120^{\circ}$.

hints: Treat $\text{Ga}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ like $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ with acid, the oxide ion forms water and the metal forms the chloride salt.
walkthrough:
Build the acid-base equation**
Here $\text{Ga}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ acts as a base. Oxide $\text{O}^{2-}$ reacts with $\text{H}^{+}$ from $\text{HCl}$ to make water, while $\text{Ga}^{3+}$ joins $\text{Cl}^{-}$ to make $\text{GaCl}_{3}$. Balancing Ga, Cl, H and O gives:
$$\text{Ga}_{2}\text{O}_{3} + 6\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{GaCl}_{3} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$

hints: Recall that $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ is amphoteric and dissolves in NaOH to give the aluminate ion $[\text{Al}(\text{OH})_{4}]^{-}$, what is the gallium equivalent?
Balance Ga, Na, O and H by adding water to the left side if you write the tetrahydroxogallate product, or write the meta-gallate $\text{NaGaO}_{2}$ alternative.
walkthrough:
Recognise amphoteric behaviour**
Like $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$, $\text{Ga}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ also reacts with alkali. It acts as an acidic oxide here, forming a soluble gallate complex, analogous to aluminate.

Write the balanced gallate equation**
With concentrated $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ the product is sodium tetrahydroxogallate:
$$\text{Ga}_{2}\text{O}_{3} + 2\text{NaOH} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaGa}(\text{OH})_{4}$$
Check atoms: 2 Ga, 2 Na, 8 O, 8 H on each side. The alternative dehydrated form $2\text{NaGaO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ is also accepted.
